Epigenetic Autism Cure

By: Eugene Botha | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Scientists use cutting edge technology to reverse a gene variant associated with autism and achieve astonishing results

Unique Selling Point:
New medical breakthrough

Summary:
A scientists in the US have found that some people with autism has a faulty gene called Shank3. This gene is switched off and causes the symptoms of autism. However, if the gene is switched on, the symptoms of autism are reversed -- even in adults. This research could spell the beginning of drugs to treat autism.

Further information:
Autism has diverse genetic causes, most of which are still unknown. Some people with autism are missing a gene called Shank3, which is critical for brain development. Without this gene, individuals develop typical autism symptoms including repetitive behavior and avoidance of social interactions.
In a study of mice, MIT researchers have now shown that they can reverse some of those behavioral symptoms by turning the gene back on later in life, allowing the brain to properly rewire itself.
“This suggests that even in the adult brain we have profound plasticity to some degree,” says Guoping Feng, an MIT professor of brain and cognitive sciences. “There is more and more evidence showing that some of the defects are indeed reversible, giving hope that we can develop treatment for autistic patients in the future.”
Feng, who is the James W. and Patricia Poitras Professor of Neuroscience and a member of MIT’s McGovern Institute for Brain Research and the Stanley Center for Psychiatric Research at the Broad Institute, is the senior author of the study, which appears in the Feb. 17 issue ofNature. The paper’s lead authors are former MIT graduate student Yuan Mei and former Broad Institute visiting graduate student Patricia Monteiro, now at the University of Coimbra in Portugal.
Boosting communication
The Shank3 protein is found in synapses — the connections that allow neurons to communicate with each other. As a scaffold protein, Shank3 helps to organize the hundreds of other proteins that are necessary to coordinate a neuron’s response to incoming signals.
Studying rare cases of defective Shank3 can help scientists gain insight into the neurobiological mechanisms of autism. Missing or defective Shank3 leads to synaptic disruptions that can produce autism-like symptoms in mice, including compulsive behavior, avoidance of social interaction, and anxiety, Feng has previously found. He has also shown that some synapses in these mice, especially in a part of the brain called the striatum, have a greatly reduced density of dendritic spines — small buds on neurons’ surfaces that help with the transmission of synaptic signals.
In the new study, Feng and colleagues genetically engineered mice so that their Shank3 gene was turned off during embryonic development but could be turned back on by adding tamoxifen to the mice’s diet.
When the researchers turned on Shank3 in young adult mice (two to four and a half months after birth), they were able to eliminate the mice’s repetitive behavior and their tendency to avoid social interaction. At the cellular level, the team found that the density of dendritic spines dramatically increased in the striatum of treated mice, demonstrating the structural plasticity in the adult brain.
However, the mice’s anxiety and some motor coordination symptoms did not disappear. Feng suspects that these behaviors probably rely on circuits that were irreversibly formed during early development.
When the researchers turned on Shank3 earlier in life, only 20 days after birth, the mice’s anxiety and motor coordination did improve. The researchers are now working on defining the critical periods for the formation of these circuits, which could help them determine the best time to try to intervene.
“Some circuits are more plastic than others,” Feng says. “Once we understand which circuits control each behavior and understand what exactly changed at the structural level, we can study what leads to these permanent defects, and how we can prevent them from happening.”
Gordon Fishell, a professor of neuroscience at New York University School of Medicine, praises the study’s “elegant approach” and says it represents a major advance in understanding the circuitry and cellular physiology that underlie autism. “The combination of behavior, circuits, physiology, and genetics is state-of-the art,” says Fishell, who was not involved in the research. "Moreover, Dr. Feng's demonstration that restoration of Shank3 function reverses autism symptoms in adult mice suggests that gene therapy may ultimately prove an effective therapy for this disease."
Early intervention
For the small population of people with Shank3 mutations, the findings suggest that new genome-editing techniques could in theory be used to repair the defective Shank3 gene and improve these individuals’ symptoms, even later in life. These techniques are not yet ready for use in humans, however.
Feng believes that scientists may also be able to develop more general approaches that would apply to a larger population. For example, if the researchers can identify defective circuits that are specific for certain behavioral abnormalities in some autism patients, and figure out how to modulate those circuits’ activity, that could also help other people who may have defects in the same circuits even though the problem arose from a different genetic mutation.
“That’s why it’s important in the future to identify what subtype of neurons are defective and what genes are expressed in these neurons, so we can use them as a target without affecting the whole brain,” Feng says.

Press Release:


Epigenetic Autism Cure
Autism is a disorder that causes suffering for millions of people, young and old. But in a promising breakthrough, scientists have found that this disorder is linked to the inadequate expression of a gene called Shank3. Carte Blanche meets the remarkable minds behind the astonishing medical technology capable of switching the gene back on and reversing the symptoms of this condition. Could a cure be imminent?


Script:


V/O
Once a year, landmarks all over the globe are bathed in blue light to raise awareness of a condition that is on the rise at an alarming rate worldwide. It has become such an epidemic that the United Nations has declared the second of April World Autism Day.
LINK:
Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and autism are both general terms for a group of complex behavioural disorders that has its origin in the development of the brain.
V/O:
People with autism have social and communication difficulties.

They may display a variety of repetitive behaviours.

It is a multifaceted condition and not all people with autism have the same level of impairment nor do they display the same symptoms.
Link:
In South Africa it is estimated that there are nearly a million people with autism – about 2% of the population, and the numbers are increasing rapidly.
Feng
And we don’t have any effective treatment for autism patients.
V/O:
Prof Guoping Feng - a Neuroscientist at the Massachussetts Institute of Technology - says traditional approaches to autism focus on treating the symptoms.
Feng:
Behaviour treatments from a very young age have been shown to have some effect in improving patients.
V/O:
But these treatments have limited success. However, Guoping’s passion for neuroscience and the brain allowed him to approach the disorder from a completely different perspective.
Feng:
All our behaviour is controlled by neuro-circuits. A group of circuits working together control individual behaviour. Whether I move my hand, whether I talk, whether singing or learning. They are all neuro-circuit controlled activities.
LINK:
And if a brain circuit malfunctions, it has a profound effect on behavioural patterns and can lead to the abnormal behaviour we see in autism.
V/O:
Guoping’s main focus is on studying how various parts of the brain communicate with each other. There are about a hundred billion neurons in the brain. Communication between them occurs when neurons fire and other neurons pick up this activity. Neurons have branch-like projections called dendrites and axons. They connect to other neurons’ dendrites and axons at tiny spaces called synapses. Here, chemicals called neuro transmitters act like messengers and transmit signals across the synapses.

Neuro-technology has developed at an incredible rate the past few years and scientists can now study brain function with enormous precision.
Feng:
We can actually label, using a fluorescent protein, a single neuron and look at their morphology, their structure. We can count how many synapses there are from other neurons.
V/O:
And they can even trace the activity of a single neuron to see if it fires to much or too little. Using this technology they are able to precisely trace faults in brain circuits.

They have found that faults in the circuits that link and allow for communication between the outer and inner parts of the brain—or the cerebral cortex and striatum—bring severe consequences.
Feng:
These regions are critical for many of our behaviours including motor behaviour including repetitive behaviours and including some of the social behaviours.
V/O:
So, faulty synapses affect behaviour. But the root cause of the faulty synapses remained unclear. They investigated further.
LINK:
In their research they were able to link the faulty synapses in this circuit to a specific gene called Shank3.
Feng
So we studied a gene called Shank3 because it’s very important for building the synapses. Building the apparatus for neurons to communicate.
V/O:
They found that if the gene is present but switched off synapses break down. This results in poor communication between the neurons of the outer cortex and inner striatum causing problematic social and behavioural patterns.
LINK:
And it is exactly these social behaviours that are at play in autism.
Feng:
That made us to conclude that defect in neuron-neuron communication is one of the key causes of autism or key pathology of autism.
V/O:
This was a breakthrough. Other scientists had in the past also established that a Shank3 mutation is linked to autism, but the exact mechanism involved remained unknown.

To confirm their findings the team explored the influence of the Shank3 gene through a battery of experiments.
LINK
Guoping decided to test this in vivo – in live animals. They decided to use mice --- for a very specific reason.
Feng:
Human Shank3 gene and mouse Shank3 gene are highly conserved. That means they are very similar.
V/O:
They needed to manipulate this gene to see what the effect would be. Fortunately a brand new gene editing technology called CrisprCas9 had become available, allowing scientists to access and alter both whole genomes and individual genes.
Feng:
We can make any kind of human mutation in mouse genome or any other species of genomes.
V/O:
Using CrisprCas9 they were able to cut the Shank3 gene from the genomes of a group of lab mice.
Feng:
In mice if you delete that gene it will cause neuro-biological change at the synapse and also behavioural change including repetitive behaviour, social interaction deficit, anxiety and these type of behaviours that we can map to a particular brain region relevant to the autism.
LINK:
With this they had proven it was possible to create mice with autism symptoms by deleting a single gene.
V/O:
The next step was to see if they could also reverse the symptoms of autism. To do this they genetically modified mice embryos. They did not delete the gene from their genomes but only flipped it or switched it off. The mice born with the flipped gene now behaved similarly to humans with a faulty Shank3 gene.
Feng:
We flip it in a way that we can treat the mouse with a compound, a drug that will flip it back to normal. So you can give the drug anytime during their lifespan and can turn the gene back on.
V/O:
The mice born with the gene that was turned off, displayed all the symptoms of autism, including excessive repetitive grooming.
Feng:
And then you can turn the gene on to see at what stage you need to turn on the gene to completely reverse the symptoms.
LINK:
They found that if you turn the gene on in adult mice their repetitive behaviours stops and they become socially normal.
Feng:
But there are also other defects we cannot reverse, so for example anxiety, motor defect. If you put the gene back in adult you cannot reverse it anymore. It’s irreversible developmental defect.
V/O:
So treating adults only reverses some of the symptoms. However, if the mice are treated when they are still very young, they are completely cured. It seems early detection and early treatment can actually prevent the disorder from developing.

Though Guoping concentrated on the Shank3 gene, in a disorder as complex as autism a host of genes contribute to its development.
Feng:
There are hundreds of genes have been identified that either cause autism or increase the risk of autism.
V/O:
This seminal work on Shank3 has underlined the role of genetics and shown that autism patterns can be reversed using drugs capable of switching on key inactive genes.

Now it remains to be seen whether the same process will work as well in humans. It could take up to ten years to achieve, but the breakthrough work done at MIT raises hope for a cure for autism that will end the need to light up global landmarks to remind the world of the daily suffering of millions.

For example, if the researchers can identify defective circuits that are specific for certain behavioral abnormalities in some autism patients, and figure out how to modulate those circuits’ activity, that could also help other people who may have defects in the same circuits even though the problem arose from a different genetic mutation. “That’s why it’s important in the future to identify what subtype of neurons are defective and what genes are expressed in these neurons, so we can use them as a target without affecting the whole brain,” Feng says.
